overview:
Kashaya-margana (kaṣāya-mārgaṇa) is a technical Jain doctrinal category found especially in the Digambara karmic and jīva-classification literature, most prominently in Acharya Nemichandra’s Gommatsara (Jīva-kāṇḍa). The compound literally means “the soul-quest (mārgaṇa) with respect to passions (kaṣāya)” and denotes the systematic way in which souls are analyzed and grouped according to the presence, type, and intensity of their passions. In this context, “margana” is not a physical path but an investigative classification scheme: a way of ‘searching out’ or ‘surveying’ the states of the soul. Kashaya-margana therefore functions as a bridge between the general doctrine of passions and the more technical karmic and guṇasthāna (spiritual stages) frameworks.

In Jain philosophy, kaṣāya—anger (krodha), pride (māna), deceit (māyā), and greed (lobha)—are the principal inner defilements that make karmic particles adhere to the soul and prolong saṃsāra. Kashaya-margana takes this basic insight and turns it into a fine-grained taxonomy: it asks, for any given soul, what kinds of passions are operative, with what strength, and with what consequences for bondage and spiritual progress. In the Digambara tradition, this is closely tied to the distinction between short-term, non-passional karmic binding and long-term, passion-driven binding. When passions are present, karmas bind for long durations and determine future births; when passions are absent or greatly subdued, karmic effects are lighter and more quickly exhausted.

Technically, Kashaya-margana is correlated with the graded intensities of passions—anantanubandhi (extremely binding, blocking right faith), apratyākhyānāvaraṇīya (severe, obstructing partial renunciation), pratyākhyānāvaraṇīya (moderate, obstructing full renunciation), and sañjvalana (mild, obstructing perfect conduct). Each intensity level is mapped to particular guṇasthānas (spiritual stages), so that the spiritual status of a soul can be read through its passion-profile. Souls dominated by anantanubandhi passions remain in the lower stages, unable to attain samyagdarśana (right faith), whereas those who have reduced their passions to the sañjvalana level can reach higher stages of right conduct and, eventually, omniscience.

Within the broader “margana” system of Gommatsara, Kashaya-margana stands alongside other soul-quests such as Kaya-margana (embodiment), Jāti-margana (genus), and so on. Each margana examines one dimension of the soul’s karmic and existential situation. Kashaya-margana is distinctive because it focuses on the inner, psychological side of bondage: not merely what body or realm a soul inhabits, but what emotional and ethical dispositions are active. This makes it central to Jain soteriology, since liberation (mokṣa) is achieved not only by external renunciation but by the progressive conquest of passions, culminating in the state of vītarāga—complete freedom from attachment and aversion.

From a practical perspective, Kashaya-margana underlines that spiritual assessment in Jainism is not based on social status or external ritual alone. A layperson with relatively mild passions may, in karmic terms, be in a better position than someone outwardly ascetic but inwardly consumed by anger or pride. The margana framework encourages introspection: one is invited to ‘survey’ one’s own inner states, recognize the specific forms of kaṣāya at work, and apply appropriate disciplines—meditation, vows, confession, and cultivation of opposite virtues—to weaken them. Modern interpreters often use Kashaya-margana to explain why Jain ethics places such emphasis on emotional regulation and non-reactivity: passions are not merely moral flaws but precise karmic mechanisms that determine the soul’s trajectory.

Scholarly and traditional discussions note that the exact enumeration and naming of marganas, as well as the detailed mapping between passion-intensities and guṇasthānas, can vary slightly between texts and sectarian lineages. Gommatsara, Dhavala, and later commentaries agree on the central role of Kashaya-margana but may differ in technical sub-classifications or in how they gloss certain terms. Because of this, careful study of primary texts and commentarial traditions is recommended, and interpretive claims should be checked against qualified teachers and established editions. Nonetheless, across these sources, Kashaya-margana consistently signifies the doctrinal insight that the inner landscape of passions is both measurable and transformable, and that understanding this landscape is essential for charting the soul’s path from bondage to liberation.

primary_sources.title: Gommatsara (Jīva-kāṇḍa), Chapter 11 – Kaṣāya-mārgaṇa
primary_sources.author: Acharya Nemichandra (Siddhānta Cakravartin)
primary_sources.original_text:
सुखदुःखसुबहुसस्यं कर्मक्षेत्रं कृषति जीवस्य ।
संसारदूरमर्यादं तेन कषाय इति मां ब्रुवन्ति ॥ २८२ ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
sukhaduḥkha-subahu-sasyaṃ karmakṣetraṃ kṛṣati jīvasya |
saṃsāra-dūra-maryādaṃ tena kaṣāya iti māṃ bruvanti || 282 ||
primary_sources.translation: “They (the Ācāryas) call ‘passion’ (kaṣāya) so because it ploughs the field of the soul’s karmas, extending to the far limit of saṃsāra and producing a vast crop of pleasure and pain.”
primary_sources.notes: This verse, cited in the Kaṣāya-mārgaṇa discussion of Gommatsara Jīva-kāṇḍa, explains why passions are termed kaṣāya: they ‘plough’ (kṛṣati) the karmic field of the soul, making karmic bondage deep and long-lasting. The surrounding chapter classifies souls according to the presence and intensity of such passions, thereby constituting the Kashaya-margana. The English rendering here follows J. L. Jaini’s translation, with minor normalization of diacritics; the underlying Prakrit/Sanskrit wording may vary slightly across manuscripts and printed editions, and some pages in available scans are noted as unproofread, so critical editions should be consulted for precise philological work.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.1–2
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation:
“Wrong worldview, non-abstinence, carelessness, passions, and activity (karma-yoga) are the causes of bondage. (8.1)
Because of passions, there is bondage of karma to the soul. (8.2)”
primary_sources.notes: Although the term ‘Kashaya-margana’ does not appear in the Tattvārtha Sūtra, these aphorisms are foundational for later Digambara analyses such as Gommatsara. They establish kaṣāya as a primary cause of karmic bondage, which Kashaya-margana then elaborates into a detailed classification of souls by their passion-states. Traditional commentaries link these sutras to the graded intensities of passions and their correlation with guṇasthānas, providing the doctrinal backbone for the Kashaya-margana scheme.

misconceptions.myth: Kashaya-margana is simply another name for the general doctrine of passions (kaṣāya) and does not add anything technical.
misconceptions.reality: Kashaya-margana is a specific classificatory framework within texts like Gommatsara that analyzes souls according to the presence, type, and intensity of their passions. While it builds on the general doctrine of kaṣāya, it introduces a structured ‘soul-quest’ that connects passion-states to karmic bondage and guṇasthānas, making it more technical than a generic discussion of emotions.

misconceptions.myth: Kashaya-margana deals only with laypeople’s ethical behavior and has little relevance to advanced spiritual stages.
misconceptions.reality: Kashaya-margana explicitly spans the entire range of spiritual development, from heavily passion-bound souls to those who have reduced passions to mild forms compatible with higher guṇasthānas. It is used to explain why certain souls can attain right faith, partial or full renunciation, and ultimately omniscience, while others remain in lower stages. Thus it is central to understanding advanced spiritual progress, not limited to lay ethics.

misconceptions.myth: Passions classified under Kashaya-margana are purely psychological and have no direct karmic consequences.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain doctrine, especially as articulated in Tattvārtha Sūtra and Gommatsara, passions are the precise determinants of long-term karmic binding. Kashaya-margana exists precisely to show how different intensities and forms of passions lead to different durations and types of karmic bondage, influencing future births and spiritual possibilities. They are not merely feelings but karmically operative states.

misconceptions.myth: Once someone adopts external ascetic practices, Kashaya-margana no longer applies to them because passions are automatically destroyed.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts emphasize that external asceticism does not by itself eliminate passions. Kashaya-margana continues to apply to ascetics, who may still harbor subtle anger, pride, deceit, or greed. Only through sustained inner transformation—meditation, vows, confession, and cultivation of equanimity—do passions diminish in intensity, allowing movement to higher guṇasthānas. The margana framework is therefore relevant to both lay and monastic practitioners.
